reason: The proposed lower-bound counting is valid after treating \(n=1,2\) separately, but its stated \(5\times5\) construction is invalid because blocks C and E overlap and the claimed hitting property fails. The periodic shifted-row construction above is disjoint, hits every triple, and incurs only an \(O(n)\) boundary correction.
text:
Take \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\). We prove the inequalities for every positive integer \(n\).

For the lower bound, suppose a maximal collection contains \(m\) disjoint removed blocks. There are \(2n(n-2)\) horizontal and vertical triples when \(n\ge3\), and maximality implies that every such triple contains a removed stamp.

A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal triples: their starting positions differ from the block's starting position by at most two. Its three stamps each belong to at most three vertical triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most fourteen potential triples. The same argument applies to a vertical block. Consequently
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
This applies to every maximal collection and hence to \(b(n)\). For \(n=1,2\), one has \(b(n)=0\), and the same inequality holds. Thus the lower bound holds with \(c=\frac27\).

For the upper bound, first consider the infinite square grid. In row \(i\), for every integer \(k\), place the horizontal block
\[
\{(i,i+5k),(i,i+5k+1),(i,i+5k+2)\}.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint. Their removed stamps are exactly the cells \((i,j)\) satisfying
\[
j-i\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
Every horizontal triple meets this set because its three values of \(j-i\) are three consecutive residues modulo \(5\), while the complement \(\{3,4\}\) has only two residues. The same argument applies to every vertical triple, for which the three values of \(j-i\) are again three consecutive residues modulo \(5\).

Now restrict to the \(n\times n\) board and retain every one of these blocks lying wholly inside it. In each row there are at most \(n/5+1\) retained blocks, so their total number is at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n.
\]
Let \(E\) be the boundary strip consisting of the first two and last two columns; thus \(|E|\le4n\). Every stamp belonging to the infinite pattern but not to a retained block lies in \(E\). Hence every triple not already hit by a retained block must meet \(E\), since every triple is hit by the infinite pattern.

Extend the retained collection greedily by adding available triples until the collection is maximal. Every added block was initially unhit and therefore meets \(E\). Since the added blocks are disjoint, they use distinct stamps of \(E\), so at most \(4n\) blocks are added. We therefore obtain a maximal collection of at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. By the definition of \(b(n)\),
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Combining the estimates proves the theorem with \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).
